questions.prompt: St. Peter instructs Christians to 'always be ready to give an explanation to anyone who asks you for a reason for your hope.' Where is this found?
choices: 1 Peter 3:15
Romans 8:28
James 2:17
1 Corinthians 13:1
questions.correctAnswer: 1 Peter 3:15
questions.explanation: 1 Peter 3:15 is the classic biblical charter for apologetics: believers are called to be ready to explain and defend the reasons for their faith, 'with gentleness and reverence.'
questions.hint: This is the go-to verse apologists cite to justify the whole discipline.

citations.quote: Always be ready to give an explanation to anyone who asks you for a reason for your hope, but do it with gentleness and reverence.

questions.prompt: True or False: According to the Catechism, faith and reason are fundamentally opposed to one another.
questions.explanation: The Catechism teaches the opposite: proofs for God's existence 'can predispose one to faith and help one to see that faith is not opposed to reason.'
questions.hint: The Catechism treats these as partners, not rivals.

citations.quote: The proofs of God's existence, however, can predispose one to faith and help one to see that faith is not opposed to reason.

questions.prompt: Some early Christians, following the heretic Marcion, argued that the Old Testament should be discarded now that Christ has come. How does the Catechism respond to this objection?
choices: It insists the Old Testament remains an indispensable, inspired part of Scripture, never revoked
It agrees the Old Testament is now optional reading
It says only the Ten Commandments from the Old Testament still apply
It says the Old Testament was only ever meant for a Jewish audience
questions.correctAnswer: It insists the Old Testament remains an indispensable, inspired part of Scripture, never revoked
questions.explanation: The Catechism firmly rejects Marcionism, the idea that the New Testament renders the Old void -- the Old Covenant 'has never been revoked' and its books retain permanent value.
questions.hint: The Church has always resisted cutting Scripture in half.

citations.quote: The Old Testament is an indispensable part of Sacred Scripture. Its books are divinely inspired and retain a permanent value, for the Old Covenant has never been revoked.

questions.prompt: The word 'apologetics' comes from the Greek 'apologia,' the same word Paul uses when he stands before a crowd in Jerusalem. What does it mean?
choices: A reasoned legal defense or explanation
An expression of regret or sorrow
A specific type of formal prayer
A term for a condemned heresy
questions.correctAnswer: A reasoned legal defense or explanation
questions.explanation: 'Apologia' means a defense, as in a courtroom -- not an apology in the modern English sense of saying sorry. Apologetics is the reasoned defense of the faith, not an expression of regret for holding it.
questions.hint: Think 'legal defense,' not 'I'm sorry.'

citations.quote: My brothers and fathers, listen to what I am about to say to you in my defense.

questions.prompt: True or False: Good apologetics means winning arguments by any means necessary, even if it requires being harsh or contemptuous toward the person you're speaking with.
questions.explanation: 1 Peter 3:15, apologetics' own charter verse, specifies defending the faith 'with gentleness and reverence' -- the manner matters as much as the content.
questions.hint: The same verse that calls for a defense also specifies the tone it must be given in.

citations.quote: Always be ready to give an explanation to anyone who asks you for a reason for your hope, but do it with gentleness and reverence.

questions.prompt: Which of these best describes the proper goal of Catholic apologetics?
choices: To remove obstacles to faith and invite a person toward the truth, not merely to defeat an opponent
To win as many debates as possible
To prove that every other religion is entirely worthless
To make faith depend entirely on winning arguments
questions.correctAnswer: To remove obstacles to faith and invite a person toward the truth, not merely to defeat an opponent
questions.explanation: Apologetics serves evangelization -- it clears away obstacles and offers reasons, but the goal is always a person's genuine encounter with the truth, not a scoreboard of debate wins.
questions.hint: The goal is an invitation, not a scoreboard.

citations.quote: Always be ready to give an explanation to anyone who asks you for a reason for your hope, but do it with gentleness and reverence.

questions.prompt: When critics claim the Trinity means Christians worship three gods, the accurate response is that the Trinity is:
choices: One God in three distinct Persons, each sharing the identical divine nature -- not three separate gods
Actually three separate gods who cooperate closely
A single Person who changes roles over time
A later invention with no basis in earlier Christian belief
questions.correctAnswer: One God in three distinct Persons, each sharing the identical divine nature -- not three separate gods
questions.explanation: The divine Persons do not divide the one divine nature among themselves -- each is fully God, and yet there is only one God, not three. This distinguishes orthodox Trinitarian belief from both tritheism and modalism.
questions.hint: The key word is 'Persons,' not 'gods' -- and there's only one nature shared, not three.

citations.quote: We do not confess three Gods, but one God in three persons, the 'consubstantial Trinity.'

questions.prompt: True or False: The Nicene Creed's claim that Christ was 'begotten, not made' means Christians believe the Son was created by the Father at some point in time.
questions.explanation: 'Begotten, not made' means the Son eternally shares the Father's own divine nature -- he was never created, and there was never a time he did not exist.
questions.hint: The Creed is drawing a contrast between 'begotten' and 'made' on purpose.

citations.quote: begotten not made, consubstantial with the Father

questions.prompt: Defending the Resurrection, apologists point to the empty tomb, the post-Resurrection appearances, and the transformation of the apostles from frightened men in hiding to bold witnesses willing to ____ for their testimony.
questions.correctAnswer: die
questions.explanation: Paul's early creedal summary in 1 Corinthians 15 lists numerous eyewitnesses to the risen Christ -- witnesses whose later willingness to suffer and die for that testimony is a striking historical detail apologists frequently cite.
questions.hint: This is the ultimate cost the apostles were willing to pay for what they claimed to have seen.

citations.quote: that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the scriptures; that he was buried; that he was raised on the third day in accordance with the scriptures; that he appeared to Cephas, then to the Twelve. After that, he appeared to more than five hundred brothers at once, most of whom are still living, though some have fallen asleep.

questions.prompt: One historical argument often made for the Resurrection is that the apostles:
choices: Were willing to suffer and die for what they claimed to have witnessed firsthand, not merely believed secondhand
Never actually claimed to have seen the risen Christ
Wrote about the Resurrection only centuries after the events
All quietly recanted their testimony before dying
questions.correctAnswer: Were willing to suffer and die for what they claimed to have witnessed firsthand, not merely believed secondhand
questions.explanation: People sometimes die for things they sincerely but mistakenly believe -- but the apostles claimed direct, firsthand experience of the risen Christ, which is a different and harder claim to explain away.
questions.hint: The key detail is that they claimed to have seen it themselves, not just heard about it.

citations.quote: that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the scriptures; that he was buried; that he was raised on the third day in accordance with the scriptures; that he appeared to Cephas, then to the Twelve. After that, he appeared to more than five hundred brothers at once, most of whom are still living, though some have fallen asleep.

questions.prompt: True or False: The virgin birth of Christ was a legend added centuries later, absent from the earliest written Gospel material.
questions.explanation: The virginal conception appears already in Matthew and Luke, among the earliest written Gospel accounts -- it isn't a late addition, even though it does appear later than Mark and Paul's earlier letters, which don't address the topic directly.
questions.hint: Two of the four Gospels record this directly, and neither is a late document.

pairs.right: Paul's creedal list in 1 Corinthians 15 is very early testimony

questions.explanation: Each objection trades on a misunderstanding of what the Creed actually claims -- careful attention to the words themselves usually dissolves the apparent contradiction.
questions.hint: Each Church response corrects a specific misreading of the Creed's actual words.

questions.prompt: Catholic apologetics responds to 'sola scriptura' (Scripture alone) by pointing out that:
choices: The New Testament itself never claims to be the sole rule of faith, and its own canon was discerned through Church Tradition
The Bible explicitly commands 'Scripture alone' in several clear passages
Tradition is a modern Catholic invention with no ancient roots
The earliest Christians had no oral teaching at all, only written texts
questions.correctAnswer: The New Testament itself never claims to be the sole rule of faith, and its own canon was discerned through Church Tradition
questions.explanation: Nowhere does the New Testament claim Scripture alone suffices -- and the very list of books making up the New Testament was itself settled through the Church's living Tradition, not by Scripture self-certifying its own contents.
questions.hint: Ask: who decided which books belong in the Bible in the first place?

citations.quote: Both Scripture and Tradition must be accepted and honored with equal sentiments of devotion and reverence.

questions.prompt: True or False: 2 Thessalonians 2:15 instructs believers to hold fast to traditions taught 'either by an oral statement or by a letter' from the apostles.
questions.explanation: This verse is a favorite apologetics proof-text: Paul explicitly places oral and written apostolic teaching on equal footing, undercutting the claim that only written Scripture carries authority.
questions.hint: Paul names two channels of teaching here, not just one.

citations.quote: Therefore, brothers, stand firm and hold fast to the traditions that you were taught, either by an oral statement or by a letter of ours.

questions.prompt: The Catechism teaches that Sacred Scripture and Sacred Tradition 'flow from the same divine wellspring' and together make up ____ sacred deposit of the Word of God.
questions.correctAnswer: one
questions.explanation: Scripture and Tradition are not two separate, competing sources -- together they form a single deposit of God's revealed word, entrusted to the Church.
questions.hint: It's a number -- the two together form only this many deposit.

citations.quote: a single sacred deposit of the Word of God

questions.prompt: The Bible's table of contents (its canon) was formally settled by:
choices: Church councils discerning, through apostolic Tradition, which books were truly inspired
A single apostle writing down a complete list before his death
A vote among ordinary lay believers across the empire
The Roman emperor Constantine at the Council of Nicaea
questions.correctAnswer: Church councils discerning, through apostolic Tradition, which books were truly inspired
questions.explanation: The canon wasn't simply self-evident -- the Church, exercising the authority Christ gave her, discerned which books were genuinely apostolic and inspired, a process later reaffirmed dogmatically at Trent.
questions.hint: Someone had to decide -- and it wasn't a Roman emperor or a popularity contest.

citations.quote: [The Synod] receives and venerates with an equal affection of piety and reverence all the books both of the Old and New Testament... as also the said traditions.
It was by the apostolic Tradition that the Church discerned which writings are to be included in the list of the sacred books.

questions.prompt: True or False: The Catholic Old Testament canon includes seven books, such as Tobit, Wisdom, and Sirach, that most Protestant Bibles exclude.
questions.explanation: These books, often called the deuterocanon, were part of the Greek Septuagint used by the early Church and were formally reaffirmed as canonical Scripture at the Council of Trent.
questions.hint: This is one of the clearest differences between a Catholic and a typical Protestant Bible's table of contents.

citations.quote: [The Synod] receives and venerates with an equal affection of piety and reverence all the books both of the Old and New Testament... as also the said traditions.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its meaning in the Scripture-and-Tradition relationship.

pairs.right: The inspired, written Word of God
God's Word handed down by the apostles, orally and in practice
The Church's living teaching office that authentically interprets both
The authoritative list of the Bible's inspired books

questions.explanation: None of these four stands alone -- Scripture and Tradition together form one deposit of revelation, and the Magisterium serves that deposit rather than standing above it.
questions.hint: One term names the written word, one the handed-down word, one the interpreting office, and one the official book list.

citations.quote: The task of giving an authentic interpretation of the Word of God, whether in its written form or in the form of Tradition, has been entrusted to the living teaching office of the Church alone.

questions.prompt: To the objection 'the Church just added books to the Bible over the centuries,' the historically accurate response is:
choices: Early councils recognized, rather than invented, books already regarded as apostolic and inspired
The full New Testament canon wasn't settled until the 20th century
Books were added by a vote of ordinary parishioners
No council ever formally addressed the canon at all
questions.correctAnswer: Early councils recognized, rather than invented, books already regarded as apostolic and inspired
questions.explanation: Local councils such as Carthage, in the late 4th century, listed the New Testament books already in widespread liturgical and doctrinal use -- they ratified an existing consensus rather than inventing a new list from nothing.
questions.hint: The word 'recognized' matters more here than 'invented.'

questions.prompt: True or False: The claim that 'Constantine invented the divinity of Christ at the Council of Nicaea in 325' is historically accurate.
questions.explanation: Belief in Christ's divinity is attested throughout the New Testament and pre-Nicene Christian writings, centuries before Constantine. Nicaea clarified and defended existing belief against Arius's denial of it -- it did not invent it.
questions.hint: The opening of John's Gospel, written centuries before Nicaea, already calls Christ God.

citations.quote: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.

questions.prompt: To the objection that 'religion and science are always at war,' apologists note that the Catholic priest and scientist Fr. Georges Lemaître first proposed what is now called the '____ Bang' theory of the universe's origin.
questions.correctAnswer: Big
questions.explanation: The Church teaches that genuine scientific research, properly conducted, can never truly conflict with faith -- a claim vividly illustrated by a Catholic priest originating one of modern cosmology's foundational theories.
questions.hint: It's the standard name for the leading scientific theory of the universe's origin.

citations.quote: Though faith is above reason, there can never be any real discrepancy between faith and reason.

questions.prompt: The 'problem of evil' objects that an all-good, all-powerful God is incompatible with the evil that exists in the world. Catholic theology responds, in part, by pointing to:
choices: The gift of human free will and the ultimate victory over evil won in Christ's Cross and Resurrection
A denial that evil really exists at all
The claim that God is not actually all-powerful
The claim that God is not actually all-good
questions.correctAnswer: The gift of human free will and the ultimate victory over evil won in Christ's Cross and Resurrection
questions.explanation: Rather than denying God's goodness or power, or denying evil's reality, the Church points to freedom's necessary risk and to God's own definitive answer to evil and suffering in the Cross.
questions.hint: The answer doesn't deny God's power or goodness, or deny evil is real.

citations.quote: There is not a single aspect of the Christian message that is not in part an answer to the question of evil.

questions.prompt: True or False: The Catholic Church has always strictly forbidden Catholics from believing in any form of biological evolution.
questions.explanation: Pope Pius XII's Humani Generis permitted Catholics to consider the theory of evolution regarding the human body, while insisting the human soul is directly created by God -- a middle position, not a blanket prohibition.
questions.hint: The Church's actual position distinguishes the body from the soul.

citations.quote: the Teaching Authority of the Church does not forbid that, in conformity with the present state of human sciences and sacred theology, research and discussions... take place with regard to the doctrine of evolution, in as far as it inquires into the origin of the human body as coming from pre-existent and living matter — for the Catholic faith obliges us to hold that souls are immediately created by God.

questions.prompt: Vatican II's decree on ecumenism, Unitatis Redintegratio, teaches that dialogue with other Christians should be marked by:
choices: Truthful charity -- respecting separated brethren while still holding to the fullness of truth found in the Catholic Church
Abandoning any claim to possessing the fullness of the truth
Avoiding all contact with other Christian communities
Treating all Christian denominations as equally authoritative on doctrine
questions.correctAnswer: Truthful charity -- respecting separated brethren while still holding to the fullness of truth found in the Catholic Church
questions.explanation: Ecumenical dialogue, as Vatican II envisions it, holds truth and charity together -- genuine respect and engagement with other Christians without dissolving the Church's own convictions about the fullness of revealed truth.
questions.hint: This kind of dialogue holds both charity and truth together, not one at the expense of the other.

citations.quote: The restoration of unity among all Christians is one of the principal concerns of the Second Vatican Council.

questions.prompt: True or False: Catholic teaching holds that people who, through no fault of their own, do not know the Gospel or the Church, can still be saved if they sincerely seek God and follow their conscience.
questions.explanation: The Catechism teaches that those who, through no fault of their own, do not know Christ or his Church, but sincerely seek God and try to do his will as known through conscience, can attain salvation.
questions.hint: The key phrase is 'through no fault of their own.'

citations.quote: Those who, through no fault of their own, do not know the Gospel of Christ or his Church, but who nevertheless seek God with a sincere heart... those too may achieve eternal salvation.

questions.prompt: St. Peter's charter for apologetics calls for defending the faith 'with ____ and reverence,' ruling out a harsh or contemptuous tone.
questions.correctAnswer: gentleness
questions.explanation: The manner of a defense matters as much as its content -- 1 Peter 3:15 pairs the call to give reasons with an explicit instruction about tone and posture.
questions.hint: This word describes the opposite of a harsh or aggressive tone.

citations.quote: Always be ready to give an explanation to anyone who asks you for a reason for your hope, but do it with gentleness and reverence.

questions.prompt: 'Interreligious dialogue,' as distinct from ecumenism, refers to engagement with:
choices: Members of non-Christian religions, such as Judaism and Islam
Other Catholic dioceses within the same country
Fellow Catholics who hold differing political views
Only self-identified atheists
questions.correctAnswer: Members of non-Christian religions, such as Judaism and Islam
questions.explanation: Ecumenism concerns unity efforts among Christians; interreligious dialogue, addressed by Vatican II's Nostra Aetate, concerns respectful engagement with non-Christian religious traditions.
questions.hint: This term is about relations beyond Christianity altogether, not within it.

citations.quote: The Catholic Church rejects nothing that is true and holy in these religions.

questions.prompt: True or False: Nostra Aetate teaches that the Church rejects nothing true and holy found in other religions, while still proclaiming Christ as 'the way, the truth, and the life.'
questions.explanation: Vatican II's declaration holds these together deliberately -- genuine openness to whatever is true and good elsewhere, without ever setting aside the Church's proclamation of Christ's unique role in salvation.
questions.hint: The document manages to affirm both openness and Christ's uniqueness at once.

citations.quote: The Catholic Church rejects nothing that is true and holy in these religions.

Dialogue and unity efforts among Christians

questions.explanation: These four activities overlap and reinforce one another, but each has a distinct scope -- knowing which is which helps a person engage each conversation appropriately.
questions.hint: One is about defending, one about Christian unity, one about other religions, one about proclaiming Christ directly.

questions.prompt: CCC 156 speaks of 'motives of credibility' that make the assent of faith 'by no means a blind impulse of the mind.' How do these motives relate to the act of faith itself?
choices: They are rational grounds (miracles, prophecy, the Church's holiness and fruitfulness) that show faith is reasonable to hold, without themselves constituting the supernatural act of faith, which remains a gift of grace assenting to God's own authority
They are identical to the act of faith itself, with no distinction between the two
They make faith entirely a matter of philosophical proof, requiring no grace at all
They are irrelevant to the act of faith and belong to a completely separate area of theology
questions.correctAnswer: They are rational grounds (miracles, prophecy, the Church's holiness and fruitfulness) that show faith is reasonable to hold, without themselves constituting the supernatural act of faith, which remains a gift of grace assenting to God's own authority
questions.explanation: CCC 156 names motives of credibility (miracles, fulfilled prophecy, the Church's holiness, fruitfulness, and stability) as external signs of revelation showing that faith is not an irrational leap -- but these motives support and accompany faith's reasonableness without themselves being the supernatural act of faith itself, which remains a free assent enabled by grace to God's own revealing authority.
questions.hint: These motives show faith is reasonable to hold; they don't replace the assent of faith itself, which is a different kind of act.

citations.quote: miracles of Christ and the saints, prophecies, the Church's growth and holiness, and her fruitfulness and stability... adapted to the intelligence of all

questions.prompt: Aquinas (ST I q.2 a.2 ad 1) distinguishes the 'preambles of faith' (praeambula fidei) from faith itself (fides infusa). What is a preamble of faith, and how does it differ from faith?
choices: A preamble of faith is a truth that can be known by unaided natural reason (such as God's existence), distinct from faith itself, which is a supernatural gift assenting to truths revealed by God that reason alone could not discover
A preamble of faith is simply a synonym for faith, with no real distinction between the two terms
A preamble of faith is a truth that can only be known through the Church's Magisterium, never through reason alone
Preambles of faith were formally rejected as heretical by the Second Vatican Council
questions.correctAnswer: A preamble of faith is a truth that can be known by unaided natural reason (such as God's existence), distinct from faith itself, which is a supernatural gift assenting to truths revealed by God that reason alone could not discover
questions.explanation: Preambles of faith are truths reason can establish on its own (God's existence, for instance) that prepare the ground for faith, but faith itself (fides infusa) is a further, supernatural gift assenting to truths -- the Trinity, the Incarnation -- that reason alone could never discover, resting on God's own revealing authority rather than philosophical demonstration.
questions.hint: One of these can be reached by philosophy alone; the other requires God's revelation and a gift of grace to assent to.

citations.quote: God, the first principle and last end of all things, can be known with certainty from the created world by the natural light of human reason.

questions.prompt: Consider this short argument: 'Nothing comes into existence without something else bringing it into existence; an infinite regress of things being brought into existence by other things is not a sufficient explanation; therefore there must be a first, uncaused cause.' Which of Aquinas's Five Ways does this instantiate?
choices: The argument from efficient causality (ex causa efficiente)
The argument from motion (ex motu)
The argument from the degrees of perfection (ex gradibus)
The argument from design/finality (ex fine)
questions.correctAnswer: The argument from efficient causality (ex causa efficiente)
questions.explanation: This argument's structure -- things being brought into existence by prior causes, requiring a first uncaused cause to avoid an infinite explanatory regress -- is specifically the argument from efficient causality, Aquinas's Second Way, distinct from the argument from motion (things being moved by other things), the argument from degrees of perfection (comparing things as more or less good/true/noble), and the argument from design (things acting toward an end).
questions.hint: This argument is specifically about things being brought into existence, not about motion, comparison of perfections, or purposeful order.

citations.quote: converging and convincing arguments, which allow us to attain certainty about the truth

questions.prompt: True or False: Dei Filius (Vatican I) condemns both fideism (the position that faith requires no rational support at all and even opposes reason) and rationalism (the position that unaided reason alone can grasp all religious truth, with no need for revelation or faith) as opposite errors.
questions.explanation: Dei Filius holds a careful middle position, condemning fideism's rejection of reason's real role in preparing for and accompanying faith, and equally condemning rationalism's claim that reason alone, without faith, suffices for the whole of religious truth -- two opposite errors the Council excludes together, not favoring one over the other.
questions.hint: The Council rejects two errors that pull in exactly opposite directions from each other.

citations.reference: First Vatican Council, Dei Filius, ch. 3
citations.quote: If anyone says that human reason is so independent that faith cannot be commanded by God: let him be anathema... If anyone says that in divine revelation there are contained no true mysteries properly so-called, but that all the dogmas of the faith can be understood and demonstrated by properly trained reason from natural principles: let him be anathema.

questions.prompt: The 'bibliographical test' evaluates an ancient text's reliability by its manuscript count and the time gap between composition and earliest surviving copy. Applying this test's vocabulary, what does the New Testament's manuscript evidence look like compared to typical ancient texts?
choices: The New Testament has a dramatically higher manuscript count and a much shorter time gap to its earliest surviving copies than the vast majority of other ancient texts routinely accepted as reliable by historians
The New Testament has a manuscript count of exactly one surviving copy, the same as most ancient texts
The New Testament's earliest surviving copy dates from over a thousand years after its composition, worse than most ancient texts
The bibliographical test cannot be meaningfully applied to any ancient religious text
questions.correctAnswer: The New Testament has a dramatically higher manuscript count and a much shorter time gap to its earliest surviving copies than the vast majority of other ancient texts routinely accepted as reliable by historians
questions.explanation: By the bibliographical test's own standard vocabulary -- manuscript count and time gap to earliest copy -- the New Testament is exceptionally well attested compared to other ancient texts (thousands of manuscripts, with some fragments dating within a lifetime or two of composition), a fact historians apply the same standard to when assessing other classical texts with far fewer surviving copies and much larger time gaps.
questions.hint: This test is meant to be applied evenhandedly -- ask how the New Testament compares by the same standard used for other ancient texts.

citations.quote: the four Gospels... faithfully hand on what Jesus, the Son of God, while he lived among men, really did and taught for their eternal salvation.

Truths reachable by unaided reason (e.g. God's existence), distinct from faith's supernatural assent
Two opposite condemned errors -- rejecting reason's role, or rejecting faith's necessity
Evaluating an ancient text's reliability by manuscript count and time gap to its earliest copy

questions.prompt: Consider a Gospel passage in which the apostles are shown fleeing in fear at Jesus's arrest, arguing among themselves about who is greatest, and Peter denying Christ three times. Which historical-critical criterion for authenticity does this material most strongly support, and why?
choices: The criterion of embarrassment -- early Christian communities would have had strong motive to omit or soften unflattering material about their own leaders, so its inclusion suggests it reflects a real, remembered event rather than later invention
The criterion of multiple attestation, since this specific detail appears independently in extra-biblical Roman sources
The criterion of dissimilarity, since no Jewish or early Christian source shares any similar language
This material fits no historical-critical criterion and provides no evidence either way
questions.correctAnswer: The criterion of embarrassment -- early Christian communities would have had strong motive to omit or soften unflattering material about their own leaders, so its inclusion suggests it reflects a real, remembered event rather than later invention
questions.explanation: The criterion of embarrassment holds that material unflattering to the early Church's own leaders and reputation is unlikely to have been invented, since the community had every motive to omit or soften it -- its presence in the Gospels, despite being awkward for the apostles' reputation, supports its historical authenticity better than criteria like multiple attestation (independent sources) or dissimilarity (unlikeness to surrounding Jewish or early Christian material), which don't directly apply to this specific kind of unflattering detail.
questions.hint: Ask why an early community, if inventing material to make itself look good, would ever include this specific detail.

citations.quote: the four Gospels... faithfully hand on what Jesus, the Son of God, while he lived among men, really did and taught for their eternal salvation.

questions.prompt: Applying the bibliographical test, how does the New Testament's manuscript evidence compare to Tacitus's Annals, a classical historical text whose reliability is not seriously questioned by historians?
choices: The New Testament has vastly more surviving manuscripts and a far shorter gap to its earliest copies than Tacitus's Annals, which survives in only a handful of manuscripts with a gap of many centuries -- the same evidentiary standard applied evenhandedly favors the New Testament's reliability at least as strongly
Tacitus's Annals has more surviving manuscripts and an earlier surviving copy than the New Testament
Neither text has any surviving manuscript evidence at all
The bibliographical test cannot be applied to Tacitus since he was not a religious author
questions.correctAnswer: The New Testament has vastly more surviving manuscripts and a far shorter gap to its earliest copies than Tacitus's Annals, which survives in only a handful of manuscripts with a gap of many centuries -- the same evidentiary standard applied evenhandedly favors the New Testament's reliability at least as strongly
questions.explanation: Tacitus's Annals, accepted by historians as a generally reliable classical source, survives in only a couple of manuscripts with a gap of many centuries to its earliest copy -- the New Testament's manuscript evidence (thousands of copies, some within decades to a century or two of composition) is dramatically stronger by the same bibliographical standard, which is exactly the comparison Catholic apologists draw to argue for treating the New Testament with at least the same historical seriousness applied to other ancient texts.
questions.hint: This level 6 skill, now applied to a specific, named comparison text rather than a general claim.

questions.prompt: A Humean objection argues that uniform human experience of natural law makes any report of a miracle inherently less credible than the alternative explanation that the witness is mistaken or lying. Using the contingency/first-cause vocabulary from level 6, what is a key weakness in this objection?
choices: The objection assumes natural law is an ultimate, self-sufficient explainer of reality, when the very contingency of the natural order (which itself needs an explanation for its existence and regularity) already points to a cause capable of acting both through and beyond that order -- 'uniform experience' can't rule out an exception by a cause not bound by the very laws it sustains
The objection has no weakness at all and is fully sound as stated
The objection only applies to Old Testament miracles, not New Testament ones
The contingency argument has nothing to do with the question of miracles
questions.correctAnswer: The objection assumes natural law is an ultimate, self-sufficient explainer of reality, when the very contingency of the natural order (which itself needs an explanation for its existence and regularity) already points to a cause capable of acting both through and beyond that order -- 'uniform experience' can't rule out an exception by a cause not bound by the very laws it sustains
questions.explanation: The Humean objection quietly treats natural regularity as needing no further explanation, but level 6's contingency argument already shows the natural order itself depends on a cause outside it -- a cause capable of sustaining the ordinary regularities of nature is not thereby bound to those regularities in every instance, meaning uniform past experience of natural law can't simply rule out, in advance, a genuine exception worked by that same sustaining cause.
questions.hint: Ask what the objection is silently assuming about whether natural law needs any further explanation at all.

citations.quote: Nothing is impossible with God, who disposes his works according to his will.

questions.prompt: The early Church grew rapidly even while facing sustained, often lethal persecution across the Roman Empire, with converts sometimes including former persecutors. Which motive of credibility does this circumstance most directly illustrate, and why does a tempting alternative fit less well?
choices: The Church's stability and fruitfulness -- sustained growth and endurance despite active, violent opposition is a stronger sign than mere numerical growth in favorable conditions would be, since favorable-conditions growth alone doesn't rule out purely social or political explanations
The motive of miracles specifically, since growth under persecution always requires a directly verified miraculous event
The motive of fulfilled prophecy specifically, since persecution itself was never prophesied
This circumstance illustrates no motive of credibility at all
questions.correctAnswer: The Church's stability and fruitfulness -- sustained growth and endurance despite active, violent opposition is a stronger sign than mere numerical growth in favorable conditions would be, since favorable-conditions growth alone doesn't rule out purely social or political explanations
questions.explanation: Growth under active persecution is a particularly strong illustration of the Church's stability and fruitfulness as a motive of credibility, precisely because ordinary social or political explanations for religious growth (favorable conditions, social pressure, political advantage) are much weaker when the visible cost of conversion was often severe -- a more targeted fit than simply invoking 'miracles' or 'prophecy' as a catch-all label for the circumstance.
questions.hint: The distinguishing feature of this scenario is growth despite real cost and danger, not a specific miraculous event or prophecy.

citations.quote: miracles of Christ and the saints, prophecies, the Church's growth and holiness, and her fruitfulness and stability... adapted to the intelligence of all

questions.prompt: Which of the following best constructs a defense of the reasonableness of Christian belief that avoids sliding into fideism?
choices: 'Christian belief rests on real motives of credibility -- historical evidence, philosophical argument, the Church's own fruits -- that show faith to be reasonable, even though faith itself remains a free assent enabled by grace, not merely a conclusion reason reaches on its own' (cf. Fides et Ratio's account of faith and reason's cooperation)
'Christian belief requires no reasons or evidence whatsoever -- it is simply believed on pure, unsupported will regardless of any rational consideration'
'Christian belief is simply whatever feels emotionally satisfying to the believer, with reason playing no role at all'
'Christian belief and reason are permanently and necessarily in conflict, with one always having to be sacrificed for the other'
questions.correctAnswer: 'Christian belief rests on real motives of credibility -- historical evidence, philosophical argument, the Church's own fruits -- that show faith to be reasonable, even though faith itself remains a free assent enabled by grace, not merely a conclusion reason reaches on its own' (cf. Fides et Ratio's account of faith and reason's cooperation)
questions.explanation: Fides et Ratio insists faith and reason are 'like two wings' working together, not in competition -- a defense avoiding fideism must actually engage real motives of credibility and rational argument, while still recognizing that the assent of faith itself is a free response enabled by grace, not a conclusion reason reaches entirely on its own the way it reaches a geometric proof.
questions.hint: The correct answer engages real reasons and evidence while still leaving room for faith as a free, grace-enabled assent -- rejecting both a reasonless leap and a reason-only account.

citations.reference: John Paul II, Fides et Ratio (1998), Introduction
citations.quote: Faith and reason are like two wings on which the human spirit rises to the contemplation of truth
